content: Currently, a significant number of individuals are affected by some form of periodontal disease. These diseases can range from mild gum inflammation to severe conditions that cause extensive damage to the soft tissues and bone supporting the teeth. In the most severe cases, tooth loss can occur. The progression or control of gum disease largely depends on the quality of daily oral hygiene practices moving forward. Causes The human mouth contains a large number of bacteria. These bacteria, along with mucus and food particles, continuously form a sticky, colorless film called plaque on the teeth. Regular brushing and flossing are essential to remove plaque. If plaque is not removed, it can harden into tartar, which cannot be cleaned by brushing alone and requires professional removal by a dentist or dental hygienist. Pathophysiology Gingivitis When plaque and tartar remain on the teeth for extended periods, they become increasingly harmful. Gingivitis, the mildest form of gum disease, is characterized by red, swollen gums that bleed easily. This condition is reversible with consistent daily brushing, flossing, and professional dental cleanings. Gingivitis does not involve the loss of bone or connective tissue that secures teeth in place. Periodontitis If gingivitis is left untreated, it can progress to periodontitis, a more severe form of gum disease. In periodontitis, the gums pull away from the teeth, forming pockets that become infected. The body’s immune response to the infection, combined with bacterial toxins, begins to break down the bone and connective tissue that hold teeth in place. Without treatment, the supporting structures of the teeth, including bone and gums, are destroyed, potentially leading to tooth loss. Risk Factors Smoking: Smoking is one of the most significant risk factors for developing gum disease and can also reduce the effectiveness of treatment. Hormonal changes in women: Hormonal fluctuations can make gums more sensitive and increase the likelihood of developing gingivitis. Diabetes: Individuals with diabetes are at a higher risk of infections, including gum disease. Other illnesses and treatments: Conditions like AIDS and cancer, as well as their treatments, can negatively impact gum health. Medications: Certain medications reduce saliva flow, which protects the mouth, making it more susceptible to infections. Others may cause abnormal gum tissue overgrowth, complicating oral hygiene. Genetic predisposition: Some individuals are genetically more prone to severe gum disease. Epidemiology and Demographics Signs of gum disease typically appear in individuals in their 30s or 40s, with men being more commonly affected than women. While teenagers rarely develop periodontitis, they may experience gingivitis. Gum disease often develops when plaque accumulates along and beneath the gumline. Natural History, Complications, and Prognosis Gum disease may be associated with other health problems, though the exact relationship remains unclear. For example, studies have shown that individuals with gum disease are more likely to develop heart disease or have difficulty controlling blood sugar levels. Women with gum disease may also have a higher likelihood of delivering preterm, low-birth-weight babies. However, it is not yet determined whether gum disease directly causes these conditions. Further research is needed to clarify these associations and whether treating gum disease can prevent other health issues. Symptoms Persistent bad breath Red or swollen gums Tender or bleeding gums Painful chewing Loose teeth Tooth sensitivity Receding gums or teeth that appear longer Physical Examination A dentist will examine the gums for signs of inflammation and use a small ruler, called a probe, to measure the depth of any pockets around the teeth. In a healthy mouth, pocket depths are typically between 1 and 3 millimeters. This procedure is usually painless. Diagnostic Studies X-rays may be taken to assess bone loss. Treatment Patients may be referred to a periodontist, a specialist in diagnosing and treating gum disease. The primary goal of treatment is to control the infection. The type and extent of treatment depend on the severity of the disease. Effective treatment requires consistent daily oral care at home. Behavioral changes, such as quitting smoking, may also be recommended to improve treatment outcomes. Deep Cleaning: Scaling and Root Planing A dentist, periodontist, or dental hygienist may perform a deep-cleaning procedure called scaling and root planing. Scaling involves removing tartar from above and below the gumline, while root planing smooths rough spots on the tooth roots to remove bacteria and prevent further accumulation. In some cases, lasers may be used to remove plaque and tartar, resulting in less bleeding, swelling, and discomfort compared to traditional methods. Medications Medications may be used alongside scaling and root planing but cannot always replace surgical intervention. Long-term studies are needed to determine their effectiveness in reducing the need for surgery. Common medications include: Prescription antimicrobial mouth rinse: Contains chlorhexidine to control bacteria, often used for gingivitis or after gum surgery. Antiseptic chip: A gelatin chip containing chlorhexidine, placed in periodontal pockets after root planing to release medication over time. Antibiotic gel: Contains doxycycline, applied to pockets after scaling and root planing, releasing the antibiotic over about seven days. Antibiotic microspheres: Tiny particles containing minocycline, placed in pockets to release the antibiotic slowly over time. Enzyme suppressant: A low dose of doxycycline in tablet form to inhibit destructive enzymes that break down gum tissue. Oral antibiotics: Tablets or capsules for short-term treatment of acute or persistent periodontal infections. Surgery If inflammation and deep pockets persist after deep cleaning and medication, surgery may be necessary. Flap Surgery This procedure involves lifting the gums to remove tartar deposits in deep pockets. The gums are then sutured back in place to fit snugly around the teeth. After healing, the gums fit more tightly around the teeth, which may make the teeth appear longer. Bone and Tissue Grafts In cases of significant bone or gum tissue loss, grafting procedures may be recommended. Bone grafting involves placing natural or synthetic bone in areas of bone loss to promote regrowth. Guided tissue regeneration may be used alongside bone grafting, where a mesh-like material is inserted to prevent gum tissue from encroaching on the bone, allowing bone and connective tissue to regrow. Growth factors, proteins that stimulate natural bone regrowth, may also be used. For gum tissue loss, soft tissue grafts using synthetic material or tissue from another area of the mouth can cover exposed tooth roots. Prevention Brush teeth twice daily with fluoride toothpaste. Floss regularly to remove plaque between teeth. Use dental tools like special brushes or picks as recommended by a dental professional. Visit the dentist routinely for check-ups and professional cleanings.
